extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of architecture, architectural historians, and informed travellers interested in Venetian palace-design
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical guidance and evaluative principles for designing, interpreting, or restoring Venetian palazzi (especially the Ducal Palace), covering proportion, light, ornament, structural treatment of angles, and decisions about rebuilding vs repair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize interior function over external symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The author argues that the architect should place elements (e.g., large windows) with 'reference to the interior of the chamber' even if this 'suffers the external appearance to take care of itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the older Venetian raised large windows to properly illuminate paintings and the council chamber rather than preserve perfect external symmetry. Anti-pattern: a modern architect 'terrified at the idea of violating external symmetry' who would sacrifice the paintings' honor and the senate's comfort by forcing symmetric external alignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light roofs and painted ceilings deliberately
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important 'to raise the light near that gorgeous roof, as well as to keep the tone of illumination in the Council Chamber serene.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce light in broad, simple masses (large windows) rather than 'many broken streams' of light from numerous small windows; position windows to favor ceiling/painting visibility and maintain a serene illumination appropriate to monumental interiors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior proportions must harmonize length, breadth, and height
rubrics_metrics.description: When an added portion requires a single chamber, 'the entire height was given to the single chamber, being indeed not too great for just harmony with its enormous length and breadth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design decisions about dividing or unifying vertical space should be driven by proportional harmony with the room's plan; prefer single lofty chambers where height complements length and breadth rather than arbitrarily subdividing into multiple floors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prominent balconies and large ground-level windows as principal ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Large windows opening on balconies (e.g. the 'Sea Balcony') are considered 'one of the chief ornaments of the palace.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place grand openings and balconies in central positions of façades to provide ornament, views, and visual emphasis; these features should be coordinated with interior function and ceremonial approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conserve important historic fabric where possible; weigh repair vs rebuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions after fires and damage should consider the value of the existing (e.g. Gothic) fabric; prominent Venetian architects pleaded to repair rather than pull down the Gothic pile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit and preserve expert opinions about safety and historic value (examples given: written opinions preserved and published); anti-pattern: enthusiastic wholesale rebuilding without regard to historic continuity, which may mark the loss of a city's characteristic period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide functional segregation to serve political and social optics
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate ranges or towers were built for prisons ('a separate tower or range of apartments was built for this purpose') to address political concerns and public perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange civic complexes so that functions with sensitive connotations (prisons, judicature) are physically separated and purposely designed to counter or control public accusations (example: prisons described here as comfortable, ventilated apartments rather than the mythic 'piombi').

rubrics_metrics.name: Break and enrich building angles; avoid unrelieved sharp corners
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the building is nearly square on plan, 'a peculiar prominence and importance were given to its angles, which rendered it necessary that they should be enriched and softened by sculpture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate visual meagreness of large façades by modifying corners through buttresses, turrets, groups of sculpture, or niches. Structural reasons (buttressing, pinnacles) and aesthetic reasons (avoid meagreness) both justify this treatment in Gothic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate principal decoration upon angles in a tiered order
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ducal Palace 'throws the main decoration upon its angles' with an arrangement: (1) enlarged lower bearing capitals, (2) figure subjects above them, (3) smaller upper capitals, (4) angels above them, (5) spiral shafts with niches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize corner sculpture as an unbroken vertical sequence from ground to top so the corner expresses the building's message and provides visual richness; follow the five-tier ordering exemplified (three great bearing capitals, figure subjects, smaller capitals, angels, spiral shafts/niches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Place ideological or programmatic statements in prominent sculptural locations
rubrics_metrics.description: The author says: 'If he has anything to say to us of the purpose with which he built the palace, it is sure to be said here' — i.e., in the corner figure sculptures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use corner figure-subjects and other prominent sculptural sites to express civic values, purpose, or dominant sentiments of the builder or polity; evaluate such works by reading their subjects as intentional statements rather than mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let historical/style-period analysis guide interpretation of fabric
rubrics_metrics.description: Venetian architecture is grouped into three principal styles (Byzantine, Gothic, Renaissance) and the Ducal Palace is composed successively of these; identifying which parts belong to which period is essential to understanding design intent and interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or restoring a complex palazzo, determine the chronological layering (which parts are Byzantine, Gothic, Renaissance) to make appropriate conservation or alteration choices; use documentary records (chronicles, archivio entries, inscriptions) to date phases and attribute works.
